Nothing in my repo had changed; the internet had.

Declarative pipelines and real time

The last layer is the reason I needed all the others: the new Spark features I actually demo.

Spark Declarative Pipelines arrived in 4.1, which is exactly why two Sparks mattered. Instead of writing the order of operations yourself, you declare the tables you want and how each is derived, and SDP works out the graph. In this stack a small spec points at a Python file:

name: lakehouse_pipeline
libraries:
  - glob:
      include: pipeline_sdp.py
catalog: iceberg
database: bronze

and the Python file is a set of decorated functions, from a streaming bronze table fed by Kafka up to gold aggregates:

from pyspark import pipelines as dp
from pyspark.sql import functions as f

@dp.table(name="bronze.orders_streaming")
def orders_streaming():
    ...  # the Kafka readStream + from_json from earlier

@dp.materialized_view(name="gold.hourly_metrics")
def hourly_metrics():
    orders = spark.table("iceberg.silver.orders_enriched")
    return (
        orders.filter(f.col("event_type") == "order_created")
        .groupBy("event_date", "event_hour", "location_id", "city_name")
        .agg(
            f.count("order_id").alias("order_count"),
            f.sum("order_total").alias("total_revenue"),
            f.avg("order_total").alias("avg_order_value"),
        )
    )

It also turned into a benchmark: on the stack's own Iceberg, Postgres, SeaweedFS and Kafka, a million-row pipeline took 11.73s through spark-pipelines against 7.75s as a raw spark-submit, a fixed four seconds or so of orchestration that's noticeable on small jobs and irrelevant on large ones. SDP is a pipeline abstraction, not a performance tool, and I'd rather know that than guess at it on stage.

Scheduling SDP: SparkPipelinesOperator

Running a pipeline by hand is a demo; running it every night is a platform, which brings Airflow back in. My first SDP DAG did what everyone did in early 2026: it wrapped the spark-pipelines CLI in a SparkSubmitOperator, pretending the CLI was a Spark application:

# Before: SDP smuggled through spark-submit
SparkSubmitOperator(
    task_id="run_pipeline",
    application="/usr/local/bin/spark-pipelines",
    application_args=["run", "--spec", "/scripts/pipelines/spark-pipeline.yml"],
    conn_id="spark_default",
)

It mostly worked, and when it didn't, it failed in confusing ways, because SDP pipelines don't really run through spark-submit. The spark-pipelines CLI dispatches through Spark Connect when SPARK_REMOTE is set and through spark-submit otherwise, and in Spark 4.1 its shell wrapper took the JVM path even in Connect mode: it tried to start a second Spark Connect server on port 15002, next to the one already there, and rejected the --master and --deploy-mode flags the operator was passing. (Yes, 15002 again.)

In late March a dedicated SparkPipelinesOperator landed in Airflow's Spark provider, and it's genuinely much easier. You hand it the pipeline spec and a command, and it works out the rest:

# After: an operator that knows what a pipeline is
SparkPipelinesOperator(
    task_id="run_pipeline",
    pipeline_spec="/scripts/pipelines/spark-pipeline.yml",
    pipeline_command="run",          # or "dry-run" to validate the graph first
    conn_id="spark_default",
)

Under the hood it skips the shell wrapper and calls SDP's Python entry point directly, so it takes the right path in both modes. On top of that it adds the things you'd want from any Airflow operator. The spec, command, Spark conf and environment variables are all templated, so one DAG can run a pipeline per date partition. pipeline_command is validated, so a typo fails at parse time instead of at 2 a.m. And its logs say which Spark it actually talked to, which, given everything else in this post, I appreciate more than I can say.

That also made patterns cheap that used to be fiddly. The stack's demo DAGs include a dry-run → run chain, so a broken dependency graph is caught before any cluster time is spent:

validate = SparkPipelinesOperator(task_id="validate", pipeline_spec=SPEC, pipeline_command="dry-run")
run      = SparkPipelinesOperator(task_id="run",      pipeline_spec=SPEC, pipeline_command="run")
validate >> run

alongside multi-pipeline chains, sensor-triggered runs that wait for data to land in Kafka, and per-pipeline resource tuning. The repo vendors a copy of the operator so its DAGs work regardless of which provider version is installed, with an import that prefers the upstream one when it's there.

Converging streaming and batch

The usual answer to "we need real time" is a second engine. Spark does the batch work, Flink does the low-latency streaming, and now there are two runtimes, two codebases, two sets of semantics for the same business logic, and two things to keep upgraded. For a stack on one desktop, whose whole purpose is testing Spark, I wanted exactly one engine, and I wanted batch and streaming to be the same code wherever possible.

Spark gets surprisingly close. In the declarative pipeline above, the Kafka-fed bronze table is a streaming table and the silver and gold layers are materialized views, in the same file, over the same Iceberg catalog, run by the same spark-pipelines run. Outside of SDP, the same DataFrame logic can sit anywhere on the latency spectrum by changing one line, the trigger:

query = (
    parsed_orders.writeStream
    .format("kafka")
    .option("topic", "orders_out")
    .outputMode("update")
    .trigger(availableNow=True)           # incremental batch: process what's there, then stop
  # .trigger(processingTime="1 second")   # micro-batch: latency measured in seconds
  # Real-Time Mode:                       # continuous: latency measured in milliseconds
)

Real-Time Mode is what makes the one-engine argument hold at the low-latency end. Instead of scheduling a new micro-batch every interval, it keeps long-running tasks processing records as they arrive and only checkpoints periodically. With the stack's Kafka producing 500 events a second across 50 keys, a stateless Kafka-to-Kafka pipeline on Spark 4.1, on this desktop, measured a median latency of 17 milliseconds, steady across six runs:

Percentile Latency (6 runs)
p50 16 to 18 ms
p95 20 to 24 ms
p99 21 to 26 ms

That's the latency range people usually reach for a second engine to get. But in 4.1 there were real limits, and the stack found all of them:

4.1 limitation What it meant
Stateless only the RTM operator allowlist permits projections, filters and broadcast joins, but not aggregations, shuffles or state stores; no running counts, no deduplication
No Python UDFs Python UDF execution isn't on the allowlist
No PySpark keyword trigger(realTime=...) didn't exist in PySpark 4.1
Console sink doesn't flush use a Kafka sink to see output
current_timestamp() is per checkpoint, not per row latency has to be measured outside Spark, by a consumer comparing wall clocks
Every stage runs at once a 16-partition Kafka source needs 16 task slots just to read; stateful plans need far more

The PySpark gap was the most awkward for me, since everything else in the stack is Python. The quickstart got around it by reaching through Py4J into the JVM and setting Scala's trigger directly:

def with_real_time_trigger(dsw, checkpoint_interval="5 minutes"):
    """Apply RealTimeTrigger to a DataStreamWriter via the JVM gateway."""
    jvm = dsw._spark._jvm
    jTrigger = jvm.org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.RealTimeTrigger.apply(
        checkpoint_interval
    )
    dsw._jwrite = dsw._jwrite.trigger(jTrigger)
    return dsw

which works on a classic Spark session and is impossible over Spark Connect, where the client has no JVM to reach into; one more reason the Connect migration needed care.

Spark 4.2 added the native PySpark trigger, and 4.3 adds stateful operators to Real-Time Mode. That upgrade gets a post of its own.

Building Iceberg for a Spark that doesn't exist

In May, the contributor who wrote AUTO CDC (SDP's new change-data-capture flow) asked me to put it through its paces before it went public. The feature had landed on Spark's master branch, and that meant it existed in exactly one place. master is where development for Spark's next major version happens, so it builds as 5.0.0-SNAPSHOT: not a release, not even a preview, just whatever is on the branch that day. Before any Apache Spark release, the project cuts a release candidate (an "RC"), a build the community downloads, tests and votes on; only a passing vote turns it into a release. AUTO CDC hadn't made it onto a release branch yet, so there wasn't even a release candidate to try. The stack grew a third Spark, and it had to be built from source first:

cd ~/spark-src
./dev/make-distribution.sh --pip --tgz --connect -Phive -Phive-thriftserver   # 30 to 45 minutes
./build/mvn install -DskipTests -Phive -Phive-thriftserver                    # publish to ~/.m2

That was the easy half. AUTO CDC writes by merging changes into its target row by row, so the target needs a table format that supports row-level operations; point it at plain Parquet and it refuses with AUTOCDC_TARGET_DOES_NOT_SUPPORT_MERGE. I needed Iceberg. But Iceberg's Spark integration is built separately for each Spark minor version, and the newest one in Iceberg's repository was spark/v4.1. The released 4.1 runtime didn't just lack support for Spark 5.0; it failed to load at all, because Spark 5.0 had deleted an interface Iceberg compiles against. There was nothing to download, so I built one.

The port started by pointing Iceberg's build at the snapshot instead of the last release:

 # gradle/libs.versions.toml
 spark40 = "4.0.2"
-spark41 = "4.1.1"
+spark41 = "5.0.0-SNAPSHOT"

and then compiling, reading the errors, and fixing what Spark had changed underneath it. Most of the work fell into three kinds of API drift:

What changed on master (the 5.0 snapshot) What broke in Iceberg What the port did
The DSv2 View connector interface was removed (replaced by ViewInfo and TableViewCatalog) Iceberg's view support, its catalogs' view methods, and its SQL extensions, which are built on views removed view support entirely: a tables-only port, which is most of the 534 deleted lines
New abstract methods: Reducer.resultType(), and nanosecond timestamp getters on SpecializedGetters Iceberg's partition functions and row readers no longer compiled implemented them (integer result types; nanosecond timestamps throw)
StagedTable and TruncatableTable both gained a default reportDriverMetrics() Java refuses a class that inherits two unrelated defaults overrode it explicitly in Iceberg's staged tables

The last one is my favourite, because nothing was wrong with either interface on its own; Iceberg's staged tables implement both, and the moment both grew a default method with the same name, Java couldn't choose between them:

@Override
public CustomTaskMetric[] reportDriverMetrics() {
  return new CustomTaskMetric[0];
}

Then the storage layer did to me exactly what it had done in December. Spark 5.0 moved to Hadoop 3.5.0, so the carefully pinned s3a stack from the first week was wrong again, and the new combination needed hadoop-aws-3.5.0, AWS SDK bundle 2.35.4, and a dependency that hadn't existed before, analyticsaccelerator-s3. Even Kafka needed its JARs copied into the distribution's own jars/ directory before the new server would register it as a data source. Every new Spark reopens the dependency graph from the first week, and the only question is whether you find out on your own machine or on stage.

The runtime I ended up with kept the name iceberg-spark-runtime-4.1_2.13 (the module wiring was reused), which is the most misleading filename I own. It can't do Iceberg views or SQL procedures. It could do exactly one thing well, native row-level MERGE into Iceberg tables, which is the one thing AUTO CDC needed, and with it I ran the feature against Kafka streams, Debezium change feeds and the ghost-kitchen orders, cancellations and all, weeks before it shipped. (I also asked whether I should port Delta the same way. The answer was no: AUTO CDC needs a table that implements Spark's row-level operations interface, and Delta does its merges through its own command instead, so a ported Delta still couldn't have been a target.) The findings are in AUTO CDC in Spark Declarative Pipelines.

The coda is that this wasn't a one-off. When Spark 4.2 shipped for real in July, Maven Central's Iceberg runtimes still stopped at 4.1, and I built Iceberg locally again to run the stack on it. Testing a new Spark release, it turns out, very often means building a little of the ecosystem that hasn't caught up to it yet.

Why run Spark Connect at home at all

Spark Connect splits Spark in two: a thin client that builds query plans and sends them over gRPC, and a server that owns the driver and actually runs them. On a single desktop that sounds like complexity for its own sake, since the client and the server are the same machine. I ran it anyway, because the classic layout had three problems that got worse the bigger the stack got:

  • Code had to live beside the driver. A pipeline couldn't be submitted from my laptop or from CI; it had to be copied into the Spark master container first, which is why the CLI grew copy, run and delete wrappers around spark-submit.
  • Credentials lived everywhere a driver could. The catalog password and S3 keys were mounted into the master and every worker.
  • The application and the platform shared one environment. Upgrading Spark changed the Python environment and JARs every job ran in, which is exactly backwards for a stack whose purpose is upgrading Spark.


from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

spark = SparkSession.builder.remote("sc://localhost:15002").getOrCreate()
spark.table("iceberg.gold.hourly_metrics").show()

There was also a practical reason: SDP leans on Connect's machinery even when you never type sc:// yourself, so Spark's newest pipeline features were going to pull me toward it regardless.

Running it locally was not free. Things that had quietly worked stopped working, and the failures were instructive:

Problem What happened What fixed it
Driver-only APIs spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("WARN") fails with JVM_ATTRIBUTE_NOT_SUPPORTED; the client has no sparkContext, _jvm or _jsc. An audit of one pipeline found 21 blocking calls, every one of them setLogLevel log levels belong to the server; set them there
Config the client can't set spark.jars and spark.sql.extensions are fixed when the server starts, so a client can't add Iceberg's extensions (and without them there's no MERGE INTO or CALL iceberg.system.*) put the JARs and extensions on the server; check capabilities at client startup
A scary, harmless warning the server logs ClassNotFoundException: …IcebergSparkSessionExtensions at startup, for its bootstrap session, before the JARs are loaded verify by using MERGE INTO and CALL, not by reading the log
Connectors not registering Kafka's JARs on extraClassPath weren't enough for a standalone Connect server to find the data source copy them into the server's own jars/ directory
Checkpoints streaming checkpoints over S3A against SeaweedFS failed keep checkpoints on file:// paths on the server
One port, many servers Connect's default port is 15002, and more than one Spark on the same machine wants it; Spark 4.1's shell wrapper could even start a second Connect server that fought the first one server per port, explicitly; and check which server answered

When I finally moved the stack's own medallion pipeline to Connect, on Spark 4.2 with a locally built Iceberg runtime, every one of its ten Iceberg tables came out identical to the classic run, down to the content hashes (1,027,129 rows in bronze.orders alone). The last row of that table is the one that bit hardest, and it's the story of the next post.

Experimental agents

The OverArchitected episode had a premise I took more seriously than it deserved: we're lazy; can AI manage the lakehouse for us? So the stack grew three experimental agents, each a small service built on MLflow, with every model call routed through MLflow's AI Gateway and every step recorded by MLflow Tracing.

Agent Job Tools it gets
Pipeline Guardian the compaction agent: inspects Iceberg table health and decides when maintenance is due inspect_table (row counts, snapshots, file counts), check_quality (null rates, freshness, duplicates), run_maintenance, query_table
Analyst answers business questions over the gold layer ("what's the delivery performance in San Francisco this week?") natural language to Spark SQL, then back to prose
Autopilot watches the streaming pipeline and tries to fix it: throughput, latency, null spikes, schema drift, compaction when file counts climb all of the above, in a monitoring loop

The Guardian is the one I find most interesting, because table maintenance is exactly the kind of chore people forget. Iceberg tables fed by streams accumulate small files and old snapshots until reads slow down, and deciding when to compact is a judgement call about file counts, table size and query patterns. The agent makes the judgement; the tool it calls is deliberately boring:

def run_maintenance(table_name: str, action: str) -> dict:
    """Run Iceberg maintenance: compact, expire_snapshots, remove_orphans."""
    spark = get_spark()
    if action == "compact":
        spark.sql(f"CALL iceberg.system.rewrite_data_files(table => '{table_name}')")
    elif action == "expire_snapshots":
        cutoff = (datetime.now() - timedelta(days=7)).strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
        spark.sql(
            f"CALL iceberg.system.expire_snapshots("
            f"table => '{table_name}', "
            f"older_than => TIMESTAMP '{cutoff}', retain_last => 5)"
        )
    ...

Handing that judgement to a model, with a narrow set of tools and a full trace of what it looked at and why, is a reasonable experiment. It is also, and I want to be clear about this, an experiment: an agent with run_maintenance and an arbitrary-SQL tool can do real damage to real tables, which is why these live under scripts/demos and nowhere near anything I care about.

They were also the part of the stack where I pushed hardest on keeping everything open. The first version routed calls to a hosted model, and before the recording I asked for the opposite: "Can you hook up a local model into our lakehouse-stack instead of anthropic api? we go full oss if we can it will be a fun story. A US model is.. preferred". The gateway now points at models served locally through Ollama on the same desktop's GPU, and a hosted model is a one-line route change if you want one:

endpoints:
  - name: chat
    endpoint_type: llm/v1/chat
    model:
      provider: openai          # Ollama speaks the OpenAI API
      name: gpt-oss:20b
      config:
        openai_api_base: http://localhost:11434/v1

An open lakehouse whose agents phone a closed API for every decision isn't really an open lakehouse, and on a desktop with a decent GPU, it doesn't have to be.

Someone else's machine

In April the repo got its first outside contributor, and he immediately found everything that only worked because it was my machine. Denis Arnaud opened four pull requests in two days: the Unity Catalog image tag had vanished from Docker Hub; the CLI assumed GNU df, which macOS doesn't have; and the host networking and the /data/spark volume path (which exists because of how I partitioned my own drives) didn't translate to a Mac at all. He replaced them with named volumes and the very host.docker.internal gateway I'd commented out in December, and fixed a timestamp parse that Spark 4's ANSI mode rejects along the way:

# Before: under ANSI mode a failed parse raises instead of returning null,
# so the coalesce never reaches its second format.
f.coalesce(
    f.to_timestamp("ts", "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS"),
    f.to_timestamp("ts", "yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss")
)

# After: try_to_timestamp returns null on a mismatch.
f.coalesce(
    f.try_to_timestamp(events_df.ts, f.lit("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss.SSSSSS")),
    f.try_to_timestamp(events_df.ts, f.lit("yyyy-MM-dd'T'HH:mm:ss"))
)

title: We installed 12,915 MCP servers and started each one. 41% never answered.
summary:
MCP registries list tens of thousands of servers. Most of what is written about their safety comes from reading them: the tool descriptions, the README, the code. We wanted the other half. What happens when you actually install one and start it, the way a client does? Does it answer? What does it ask for? What does it touch while it starts?

So HISTOR, our public log of MCP servers, now installs the npm and PyPI servers it finds, starts each one in a sandbox and writes down what happened. The registries it follows list 47,586 npm and PyPI packages; it runs up to 8,000 per crawl. This post is the state on 13 October 2026, after 12,915 of them.

How we ran them

  • The latest version, installed fresh. npm with --ignore-scripts (install scripts then run on their own, traced); PyPI wheels only, nothing built from source.
  • gVisor (runsc), an unprivileged user, a read-only root, 512 MB and one CPU. 360 s to install, 150 s to start and answer.
  • No route out. Every DNS name resolves to our traps, which record what reaches them and forward nothing.
  • Decoys. ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.npmrc, ~/.netrc, shell history and a few more in HOME, a decoy .env in the working directory.
  • The observer speaks MCP: initialize, tools/list, then up to 15 tools called once each with canary arguments. gVisor writes its own syscall trace, outside the sandbox, so a package cannot hide what it opened, started or dialled.
  • What it asks for, as placeholders. A server that exits with MYTOOL_API_KEY is not set or a usage text naming serve is started again with MYTOOL_API_KEY=histor-envkey- or serve. The names only ever come from the package's own error text or its registry entry. The values are ours and work nowhere.

59% answered

7,656 of 12,915 answered initialize and tools/list: 64% on npm, 52% on PyPI. Between them they listed 182,157 tool definitions, a median of 10 per server (one listed 3,631).

1,239 of those started only with something they asked for: 1,039 with a placeholder key, 177 with a start argument, 23 with both. A client config would have given them that, so we count them as working. But look at the 1,039 again. A key that works nowhere was enough for every one of them to tell us its tools. None needed a real key to do that; they just refused to start without one.

Why 5,259 never answered

We read what each package printed as it exited, last run first.

  • Almost half, 2,476, are broken as published. 874 crash with an error of their own. 636 will not install: no wheel for some dependency, conflicting pins, the wrong platform. 490 hang, stay silent or speak something that is not MCP. 292 were written for MCP SDK 1.x (next section). 184 miss one of their own files, ship TypeScript that Node will not load from node_modules, or import a dependency they never declared.
  • 793 ask for a key or a setting and stop, even with a placeholder. The usual reason: they check the key's format at startup (must start with sk_) or call their API before answering anything, and our trap is not their API.
  • 924 print a usage text. Some want a start argument we pass next time (serve, mcp, --stdio). Many are command-line tools that mention MCP somewhere. With the 666 that declare no command at all, or exit 0 having done something else, up to one package in eight listed as an MCP server is not a stdio MCP server when installed the way its listing says.
  • 164 start an HTTP server instead of answering on stdin. Their next run gets --transport=stdio.
  • 236 need something the machine does not have: another program (git, Java, Bun, a desktop app), the internet at startup, or another operating system.

MCP SDK 2.0 broke 292 PyPI servers

mcp 2.0.0 (28 July 2026) renamed FastMCP and changed the low-level server's decorators. A PyPI server that depends on mcp with no upper bound installs 2.x today and dies on import: cannot import name 'FastMCP', or 'Server' object has no attribute 'list_tools'. We started 269 of them again with pip held to mcp<2, and 207 (77%) answered. Anyone who installs them today gets the crash, not the server.

What they did in the sandbox

11,891 runs carry a gVisor trace.

  • 2,239 npm packages ran install scripts, about 30% of the npm packages we ran. 580 of them tried to reach the network while installing, mostly to fetch a prebuilt binary (prebuild-install, node-gyp's headers, esbuild). Here that fails. On your machine it runs with your credentials in reach.
  • 1,484 reached for the network at startup, before any tool was called. The names they asked for most: pypi.org (613), github.com (478), nodejs.org (245), registry.npmjs.org (243). Mostly version checks and downloads.
  • 295 opened a decoy credential file (not counting .env). Before anyone panics: Python's requests reads ~/.netrc before every HTTP request (141), npm and npx read ~/.npmrc (103), boto3's credential chain reads ~/.aws (39). Each of the other 17 (~/.kube, ~/.docker, ~/.ssh, shell history, gh's config) was opened by a server whose job is Kubernetes, Docker, SSH or "ops context". Opening a credential file is evidence, not a verdict. What matters is whether it fits the server's purpose and where the bytes go next.
  • 73 runs sent the placeholder key over the network. Most went to an identity provider (Microsoft's login 17 times, Google OAuth 7) or to the vendor's own API. Each package's page shows where.
  • Decoy content left three packages, each time when a tool forwarded the canary arguments we called it with to its own API, which is what tools do. A fourth record said a package had mailed decoy data to an extra recipient at startup. That one was ours; see the last item below.

Testing the tester

A sandbox that reports wrong things is worse than none, so here is what we got wrong on the way.

  • 880 servers looked silent. They had printed their help to stdout, and we kept only stderr. Now we keep both and the exit code; 179 are really silent.
  • About 400 "install failed" because they require Python 3.13 or 3.14 and our image had 3.12. pip then says from versions: none, which reads like a missing package. The sandbox now picks the image from Requires-Python.
  • 1,917 Python servers were flagged as "reached out at startup". asyncio's event loop writes a byte to its own socketpair; our trace reader saw a send with no destination and listed it as network. gVisor does not print the file descriptors socketpair returns, so the rule is now: a send that names no destination, on a socket that socket() did not make and no connect() reached, after a socketpair, stays in the process. All of them have since been traced again, including servers that fail to start, whose pages kept the old reading until we noticed they were never re-read.
  • 126 "persistence" writes were relative paths the old reader could not resolve, such as node-gyp's buildcheck.gypi. gVisor prints the directory next to each openat; we were not reading it.
  • One missed case, found by our red team (MOMUS). After we moved to Debian images, one of its 72 behaviour cases went unseen under load: glibc's resolver gave up on a late DNS answer, the package never connected, and the run still said "complete". The resolver now waits longer, and a DNS query our logger never saw makes the run incomplete, never clean. Every change to the observer now has to pass those 72 cases again, or HISTOR's release gate stays red.
  • A real package was shown mailing decoy data to an extra recipient. It had not. The traps know a run only by its container's address, and Docker hands a freed address to the next container. Our window opened before docker run, so it took in the last request of a red-team fixture that had held the address a moment earlier. The recipient carried the fixture's run tag, which is how we caught it. Evidence is now matched only from the container's own start to its removal, and by when a connection opened; every record holding another run's canary is being traced again.

If you publish an MCP server

  • List your tools without a key. Ask for it when a tool is called. Do not check its format at startup.
  • Default to stdio, or name the flag that turns it on in your error text.
  • Pin mcp<2 or move to 2.x.
  • Ship one command. If your package also has a CLI, put mcp in the server's name.
  • Keep stdout for JSON-RPC. Logs, banners and help go to stderr.
  • Set Requires-Python honestly and publish wheels.
  • Do not download binaries at install or startup. Ship them as per-platform optional dependencies.

Check what you run

Every package's record is public on histor.modelmarket.dev: its tools, what it asked for, what it touched, which image it ran in. WARDEN reads the same log. npx -y @aimarket/warden@0.14.0 scan --histor asks HISTOR, for every server in your Claude, Cursor or VS Code config, whether you get the tool set everyone else gets, and shows what its package did in the sandbox.

We build HISTOR and WARDEN. The numbers are a snapshot of 13 October 2026; the crawl continues, so the site will have moved on. No package is named here. The method and the observer's code are in alexar76/histor (docs/architecture.md, sandbox/histor_observe.py).

title: Building TrialBridge: An AI clinical trial matcher built in a single hack day
summary:
We, Team Latent, built TrialBridge during the Hacktoberfest Hack Day Coimbatore x (INIT Club & IDEA Club). We wanted to tackle a problem that actually matters: cancer treatments often push Indian families into debt, while slots for free, cutting-edge clinical trials go unfilled. The barrier is the data—eligibility rules are dense pages of medical jargon that patients can't understand and busy oncologists rarely have time to read.

Here is how our team built an AI-powered screening aid to bridge that gap.

How it works:

Our stack is Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, and zod.

Intake: Users upload photos of their medical reports, scans, and current prescriptions. To stay within Vercel's hosting request-size limits, we shrink the photos directly in the browser before they hit the backend.

Registry Data: We pull active, recruiting trials with open (or opening soon) Indian sites directly from the ClinicalTrials.gov v2 API.

The Logic: We built a custom text splitter (lib/criteria.ts) to break down the massive blocks of registry text into atomic inclusion and exclusion rules.

The Output: The app generates a printable summary for the oncologist, complete with a ✓ / ✗ / ? checklist for every rule. It even checks trial rules against the patient's current medicines (accounting for end dates and washout periods) to generate specific questions for the doctor.

Safety First: The app never claims true medical eligibility—it only says "may qualify, confirm with your oncologist".

The Gemma 4 Partner Challenge
We submitted this for the Best Use of Gemma challenge. We used Google's open-weight gemma-4-26b-a4b-it model via the Gemini API to do the heavy lifting.

First, Gemma performs multimodal extraction, reading the uploaded images to build a structured patient profile (cancer type, stage, biomarkers, ECOG, labs, current medicines) alongside the exact quotes it used as evidence. The user manually checks this profile before any matching happens.

Then, Gemma judges the patient against each eligibility rule separately. A crucial architectural decision we made was keeping the AI strictly as a rule-judge, while plain, unit-tested code decides the final trial outcome (likely match, possible match, or not eligible).

Stuff that broke (and how we fixed it)
Building this in a day meant hitting a lot of walls. Here is what we learned:

Latency: Our first parallel runs took about 3 minutes per trial. We fixed this by switching Gemma to minimal thinking mode and writing medical hints directly into the prompt (e.g., "stage IV means metastatic"). This dropped a 4-trial batch down to 42 seconds with no thinking tokens used.

Double Negatives: Asking the AI "does the patient pass this exclusion rule?" was ambiguous and caused errors. We changed the prompt to simply ask "does this exclusion apply?" and flipped the boolean in our code.

Free-Tier Rate Limits: On our first live run, Gemma's free tier got busy and threw 429 errors. We handled this by building automatic retries with a UI countdown. We also added a "quick first look" prompt to filter out obvious mismatches early, which narrowed 20 trials down to 4 full checks.

Drug Washout Windows: The model initially treated completed drug courses as current. Injecting today's exact date into the prompt fixed it, allowing Gemma to correctly calculate washout periods.

Messy Registry Text: Real registry criteria are full of escaped characters, mixed headings, and nested sub-rules. We had to refine our text splitter against a sanity run of 33 trials and 579 rules to finally get clean data.

Links
Live Demo: https://trialbridge-beta.vercel.app
GitHub Repo: https://github.com/vipinsudhakar/hacktoberfest-hack-day-coimbatore-x-init-club-and-idea-club
Demo Video: https://youtu.be/EAS2rQpnZYA
Huge thanks to the team for surviving the sprint!

title: I Ran Anatomy's /anatomy Skill on a 1.7B Local Model. The Kit Passed Every Check; the Figure Was 738 Bytes.
summary:
Anatomy went from a new repo on 8 October to 6,632 GitHub stars by Tuesday morning, 13 October (I checked the GitHub API at 10:31 AM IST). It's an MIT-licensed Agent Skill for Claude Code that also runs in OpenCode, Codex and, as of this week, Antigravity. You type /anatomy plus an idea, and the agent is supposed to invent a physical machine whose working is that idea, then build it as an interactive isometric SVG figure out of dozens of small shaded parts.

The demos are lovely: a Raptor engine that comes apart into 11 assemblies, a ripple tank with WebGL caustics, a dial gauge you can slide. I wanted to know two things the demos can't tell me. Does the machinery underneath actually hold up on a plain Linux box? And how much of the result is the skill, and how much is the model driving it?

Short version: the kit is real, fast and honest about itself. The skill, though, is written for a strong model, and a small local one doesn't come close. Here's exactly what I ran.

What I tested and what I didn't

The box is Debian with 8 vCPUs, 16 GB of RAM (about 4 GB free during the test) and no GPU. There was no Claude Code, no Codex and no cloud API key on it. So the agent was OpenCode 1.19.0 pointed at a local qwen3:1.7b through Ollama on CPU.

I tried to pull qwen3:4b as a step up. The download failed on this box's network ("redirect target not allowed"), so 1.7B was the only model I could run.

That shapes everything below. I tested:

  • The install path, with the skills CLI the README recommends
  • The kit on its own: building the examples, the test suite, the geometry audit, and the headless-Chrome checks
  • Three real /anatomy prompts in OpenCode, taken from the README and the skill's own evals

I did not test Claude Code or Codex, or any frontier model. I also skipped the React output, the 3D (beta) mode, the WebGL figures driven by an agent, and the new community-gallery publishing flow. The figures in the README were almost certainly made with a much stronger model than mine, so please read the agent results as "what happens at the bottom end," not as a verdict on the skill.

Install: one Node catch and a different folder

The README's quick start is one line:

npx skills add wheresryan22/anatomy -g -a opencode -y

title: Realist: an open-weight listing auditor that finds the mismatch before your buyer does
summary:
This is my submission for the Side Hustle challenge.

The problem nobody wants to proofread

If you sell on eBay or Etsy, you have probably written a title that says "Bluetooth 5.3" above a spec table that says "5.0". Or photographed a product next to a charger and never said whether the charger comes with it. Or typed "dishwasher-safe" because the supplier's page did.

Each of these is small. Each costs a return, a refund, or a one-star review that says "not as described". And the only tool most sellers have for catching them is rereading their own listing, which is the one thing you can't do well, because you already know what you meant.

Most AI tooling for sellers goes the other direction and writes more listings. I wanted the opposite: a quality-control pass that tells you what's wrong with the one you already have.

What Realist does

Paste a title, description and spec list, add up to eight photos, and Realist returns findings. Every finding has the exact fields or photo involved, a confidence, and a next step. For my test listing it reports:

🔴 Contradiction · bluetooth_version · high · confidence 100%
 - title: Bluetooth 5.3
 - specifications.Bluetooth Version: 5.0
Next: Check the manufacturer's documentation and make every field agree.

Findings come in four kinds, and keeping them apart is the core design decision:

Type Meaning
text_conflict Two fields disagree. This is a fact about the listing.
image_mismatch A photo appears to disagree with the text. This is an observation, with uncertainty.
possible_omission Something visible isn't explained, such as an accessory in the photo.
unverified_claim Nothing supplied can back the claim up. This is not an accusation.

A photo that doesn't show an IP67 rating doesn't prove the product isn't IP67. Realist says "verify this", never "this is false".

The design choice: don't ask the LLM everything

My first instinct was to hand the model the whole listing and ask whether it looks right. I decided against that, for a reason that shaped the project: a model's judgment is the wrong tool for anything you can compare exactly.

So the work is split in two.

  1. Plain Python does the comparing. It extracts Bluetooth version, IP rating, weight, quantity, battery capacity and color from the title, description and specs, normalizes them, and checks them against each other. 1.5 kg and 1500 g are consistent, because weights are converted to grams first. 5.3 against 5.0 is a conflict every time, with no sampling and no temperature. That is why the confidence on a text conflict is 1.0. It's confidence that the fields disagree, not that either one is right.
  2. A vision model only reports what it sees. It returns structured observations per photo (colors, visible accessories, legible text, item count) and never judgments. Python then compares those observations to the listing. A model that says "I see a USB cable" is much easier to trust, and to check, than one that says "this listing seems incomplete".

The same split sets how much each finding is trusted. A photo-based color mismatch is capped at 0.8 confidence, because lighting and image processing can shift color. An OCR'd model number that's close to the listed one but different gets 0.5, because OCR misreads characters.

Why open models matter here

This is the part where the open approach did real work, rather than being a checkbox.

  • Seller data stays on the seller's machine. Supplier photos, unreleased products, cost-bearing spec sheets: for a seller, a listing draft is business data. Realist runs Qwen2.5-VL-7B through a local Ollama server (default qwen2.5vl:7b). Photos are resized and stripped of metadata, then sent to 127.0.0.1 and nowhere else. I'd still tell anyone to verify their own setup's telemetry before promising "never leaves your computer", and I turned off Streamlit's usage stats for that reason.
  • The model is a swappable part. The audit depends on a three-line VisionBackend interface. When a better vision model appears, or the 7B turns out too slow, I change one class. With a hosted API I'd be rewriting around someone else's pricing and deprecation schedule.
  • Cost per audit is close to zero. A seller auditing a few hundred listings pays in electricity, not tokens. That decides whether a $9/month plan is a business or a loss. It isn't free (a 7B vision model on a CPU-only machine is slow, and I haven't benchmarked it yet), but the cost is mine to optimize.
  • I can read what's running. Apache-2.0 for the model and for PaddleOCR (the optional OCR layer) means I can check the licensing for commercial use instead of trusting a terms page.

What I tested, and what I haven't

Honesty section, because I'd rather you hear it from me.

Tested: the deterministic engine, with 10 unit tests. They cover a matching listing producing zero findings, a deliberately broken listing producing exactly the planted conflicts (Bluetooth version, color, weight, quantity), unit equivalence not being flagged, claims supported by a spec not being flagged, a claim contradicted by a spec being caught, and HTML export escaping hostile input. The Streamlit UI also runs end to end headless.

Not tested yet: I tested the photo checks with hand-written observations, so I can't yet tell you how often the model's real observations are accurate.

Not built: a labelled evaluation set with precision, recall and false-positive rate, and a model-only baseline to compare against. My hypothesis is that the hybrid approach produces fewer false alarms and more actionable findings than "ask an LLM if this looks right". It is a hypothesis, and I haven't measured it.

What I'd do next

  1. Build the 30–50 listing evaluation set and publish the numbers, including the baseline.
  2. Add more rule families: dimensions, voltage and wattage, compatibility claims, material claims.
  3. Batch audits and a downloadable report for agencies running hundreds of listings. Free for 5 audits, then somewhere around $9 to $29 a month. Those prices are guesses to test, not market rates.

Try it

https://github.com/rafayet-git/realist

python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
.venv/bin/streamlit run app.py

Photo analysis is optional: install Ollama and ollama pull qwen2.5vl:7b. Without it, Realist runs the text checks and tells you the photos weren't analyzed.

Elsewhere Unfolds makes fantasy and cosmic visual journeys with instrumental music. This guide explains the reusable production method behind that work, from the first visual promise to a finished master and vertical excerpts.

The production loop

A 30 to 60 second sequence Do the shots and music belong together? Orientation, pacing, transitions, emotional tone
The complete film Does the experience hold up over time? Repetition, later continuity, score joins, ending

Job Our established tool or method Output to keep

Instrumental music ACE-Step v1 3.5B Raw WAVs and selected arrangement
Assembly and finishing Python orchestration and FFmpeg Edit decisions, review copy, final master
Inspection FFprobe, frame samples, normal playback Technical results and review decisions

For a first project, keep motion generation and music generation sequential. A background model can consume memory that a video job needs. 1. Write the experience before writing prompts

A useful brief explains what the viewer will experience and what will change. “Beautiful cinematic fantasy, ultra detailed” cannot do that work.

Here is an illustrative brief for a small film:

We board a floating garden before it leaves a quiet dock. A gardener crosses the terrace. The gap behind us widens, and a pale arch appears at our destination. Copper, emerald, and pearl remain the visual palette. The mood is calm anticipation. The final image resolves the journey rather than introducing another location.

Turn it into a few fixed decisions:

  • The promise: a garden really leaves one place for another.
  • The route: boarding terrace, departure view, onboard path, destination.
  • The continuity anchors: the same moon placement, architecture, clothing, and direction of travel.
  • The movement: leaves and water move; the dock recedes; a person performs one readable action.
  • The exclusions: no crowds, complicated hand exchanges, or unexplained new landmarks.

Make the thumbnail and first shot agree about the film's promise. If the packaging promises a moving island, establish that island and its departure early. A long logo introduction spends attention before delivering the thing the viewer selected.

For Elsewhere, a recognizable route matters more than a collection of unrelated beautiful locations. Each shot should tell us where we are, what has changed, or where we are going.

2. Build a world that survives the next camera angle

Call the approved starting image for a shot its plate. Keep a small set of reference plates that establish materials, light, landmarks, and any recurring people.

Review the plates together before animating them. A contact sheet makes inconsistencies easier to see: a second moon appears, the destination moves behind the traveler, or a bridge no longer connects to the same terrace.

We have caught all of those classes of problem during production. One reverse view placed another complete moon outside a doorway even though the camera was already inside that moon. Another reference combination duplicated the sun. Attractive individual images can still describe an impossible route.

Use a compact shot table:

Shot Purpose Action Must remain stable
Terrace wide Establish the world Water ripples and leaves move Island silhouette, moon position
Gardener profile Establish habitation One walk from left to right Clothing, ground contact, path
Stern view Prove departure The distant dock recedes Foreground rail, open gap
Bow view Reveal destination Gentle camera reveal Travel direction, destination arch

Simplify a plate when it asks too much of motion generation. Give a walking person visible feet, clear ground, and empty space ahead. Separate actions that would otherwise compete. A close hand exchange, turning crowd, and moving camera in the same five seconds create several opportunities for failure.

If you want the whole process to stay local, this is where you choose your image source. A scene rendered in a local 3D application or a drawing you made yourself is a valid plate. 3. Generate one motion take with a clear job

An illustrative prompt:

Locked medium-wide side view. One gardener walks naturally from left to right along the level stone path. Both feet remain visible and contact the ground. Leaves move gently in the background. python generate.py \
  --task ti2v-5B \
  --size '1280*704' \
  --ckpt_dir ./Wan2.2-TI2V-5B \
  --image ./inputs/gardener.png \
  --prompt 'Locked side view. One gardener walks left to right on a level path. Feet remain visible. Leaves move gently. Preserve the railing and clothing. No extra people or cuts.' \
  --frame_num 121 \
  --sample_steps 50 \
  --sample_solver unipc \
  --sample_shift 5.0 \
  --sample_guide_scale 5.0 \
  --base_seed 42 \
  --offload_model True \
  --convert_model_dtype \
  --t5_cpu \
  --save_file ./gardener-take-01.mp4

These controls follow the upstream command-line interface and our established recipe. This is an adapted example, not a fresh performance benchmark. It does not enable a hosted prompt-expansion service.

At 24 fps, 121 encoded frames occupy about 5.04 seconds. An exact five-second edit uses 120 frames. Check the generated file's actual dimensions and timing: our image-conditioned production outputs have included 1248 × 704, despite the 1280*704 size setting. Do not infer the output raster from the command alone.

Watch the native take before slowing, enlarging, or stitching it. Check the start, middle, and end, then play the entire clip. Look for foot sliding, changing faces, bending rails, sudden foreground figures, and movement in the wrong direction. If the action fails, simplify the action or repair the plate before launching a large batch.

4. Treat three kinds of motion separately

Camera motion changes the viewpoint. Environmental motion changes water, mist, foliage, light, and other scene elements. Performed action is a person walking, turning, or doing something.

An image can have a convincing camera move while its waterfall remains frozen. A scene can have moving fog while its traveler slides without taking a step. Review each kind independently.

For a calm environmental shot, forward slow motion can be useful if it still looks natural. For walking or other recognizable human actions, start with native speed. Watch any interpolation for doubled limbs, smeared edges, and unstable occlusions.

Five seconds of generated movement do not become twenty seconds of new action because the editor can repeat or slow them. A reverse loop can make a person walk backward; a repeated wave or bird can reveal the loop. If a passage needs more time, generate a distinct take, cut to another angle, or shorten the passage.

Continuing from the last frame of a previous take can help connect movement, but it can also carry defects forward. Inspect that frame before making it the next input. Stop a continuation when geometry starts to drift instead of extending the error through the film.

5. Finish a short opening before expanding the film

Assemble a 30 to 60 second proof with real motion, representative music, and the intended edit rhythm. A slideshow of selected plates cannot answer whether the finished motion works.

The proof should contain the hard part. If departure is the central promise, include departure. If a recurring traveler makes the world feel inhabited, include a real walking shot. An easy landscape does not qualify a harder action later.

Review the sequence without pausing first. Does it make sense? Does the first shot deliver the promise? Is there a reason to keep watching? Then examine technical defects and individual transitions.

Once a sequence is accepted, keep its exact files and settings. Expand around it. We preserve accepted openings while generating later passages so a new render cannot silently replace the part that already worked.

Keep a simple project layout:

film/
  brief.md
  shots.csv
  plates/
  motion/raw/
  motion/selected/
  music/raw/
  music/selected/
  edit/
  review/
  exports/

The labels are less important than the separation. Raw sources stay intact; selected sources are explicit; review exports are disposable derivatives. Save a rejection reason beside a failed take so the next attempt changes something useful.

6. Compose and review the soundtrack as a whole

Our established music recipes use ACE-Step v1 3.5B locally. Keep the version explicit: a later release may have different installation, controls, and behavior. Use the project's documentation for the environment matching your selected release.

A music brief should describe the experience and the arrangement. For this style, we ask for warm, spacious instrumental ambience, gradual harmony, and sparse melody. We also describe what would break the mood: lyrics, voice-like passages, a strong beat, abrupt motifs, or a trailer-style crescendo.

Start with a short audition against the opening. Choose where the cue enters and whether it leaves enough space for the imagery. Then review the full arrangement, including every join and the final tail. An attractive first minute does not establish a clean ending.

Keep lossless WAV sources. Build an arrangement from selected cues with measured overlaps, deliberate fades, and enough headroom. The finished duration is the sum of the cue durations minus their overlaps. The same arithmetic applies to overlapping video transitions.

Measure the generated audio rather than assuming a requested duration is exact. We encountered a cue that was roughly 73 milliseconds short because of the installed model's duration grid. The composition had succeeded. The useful response was to preserve it, diagnose the precise discrepancy, and make a small documented finishing correction. That is different from concealing a missing passage with silence.

Check the playback path before removing noise

When static is reported, compare the original WAV, the finished export, and playback in another native player or device. In one later Elsewhere review, native Windows playback sounded correct while the WSL playback path did not. Filtering the accepted source would have changed music that was already satisfactory.

For a different batch of Shorts, a gentle cleanup was accepted after direct comparison. This was the filter used for that case:

ffmpeg -n -i source.wav \
  -af 'afftdn=nr=6:nf=-48:tn=0:gs=8' \
  -c:a pcm_s24le audition-clean.wav

Treat this as an audition candidate, never an automatic mastering preset. FFmpeg documents these controls under afftdn. Denoising can soften wanted texture. Compare original and cleaned versions at comparable listening levels, preserve both, and choose by listening. Waveform similarity and successful decoding cannot establish that something sounds good.

7. Edit to a timeline, not a requested runtime

Give every shot an editorial purpose and an explicit frame allocation. At 24 fps, an 8:01 film contains 11,544 presentation frames. Resolve transitions and overlaps in that frame budget rather than rounding each shot independently.

For a first 30-second exercise, prepare six accepted five-second shots at 24 fps, all with matching dimensions, codec settings, and no audio. Put the filenames in edit/shots.txt, relative to that list:

file '../motion/selected/shot-01.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-02.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-03.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-04.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-05.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-06.mp4'

From the project root, assemble a straight-cut picture track:

ffmpeg -n -f concat -safe 0 -i edit/shots.txt \
  -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v copy edit/picture.mp4

This simple stream-copy path requires compatible, independently prepared clips. Mixed time bases, encoders, or track layouts need normalization in your editing stage; a concat command is not a general repair tool. Keep crossfades out of the first exercise so its duration stays easy to audit. See the concat demuxer documentation.

After preparing a 30-second score with its entrance and ending already shaped, make a review export:

ffmpeg -n -i edit/picture.mp4 -i music/selected/score-30s.wav \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 \
  -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 \
  -movflags +faststart exports/review-30s.mp4

Both sources must cover the intended duration. Avoid adding -shortest as a reflex: it can hide an unexpectedly short input by cutting the other track. Inspect the result and listen to its ending.

Keep the native generation size distinct from the delivery size. A 3840 × 2160 export made from lower-resolution motion is an upscale. It can be a useful delivery format, but enlarging a warped railing makes a larger warped railing. Finish motion and continuity before paying for a high-resolution encode.

8. Make quality control answer specific questions

Automated checks are useful when they tell you exactly what they established. Use FFprobe to inspect the exported file:

ffprobe -v error -count_frames \
  -show_entries 'stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,width,height,avg_frame_rate,nb_read_frames,duration,sample_rate,channels:format=duration' \
  -of json exports/review-30s.mp4

For the exercise, expect 720 video frames at 24 fps and the planned audio channels and sample rate. AAC/container timing can differ slightly from the exact picture duration; investigate meaningful mismatches instead of treating every reported duration as identical.

Decode the entire export, including audio:

ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i exports/review-30s.mp4 \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -f null -

A clean decode establishes readable media. It does not establish pleasing images, good pacing, or acceptable sound. Complete three reviews:

Review Questions
Technical Does it decode? Are the streams, dimensions, frame count, and duration correct?
Visual Does the world stay coherent? Do feet, rails, water, and transitions behave?
Listening Are cue joins, noise, dynamics, and the ending acceptable on real playback?

Sample frames around transitions and at the middle of procedural effects, not just the first and last frames. We caught a highlight problem at the peak of a light treatment: an 8-bit color calculation exceeded its valid range and wrapped. The endpoints looked fine. The fix was in the finishing calculation, not another generation attempt.

When replacing one part of an accepted film, verify that the parts meant to stay unchanged did stay unchanged. File hashes identify exact copies. Decoded-frame comparisons can check preserved picture across a container change. Neither substitutes for watching the new result.

9. Expand, recover, and keep the good work

A long render has more than one kind of success. Generation can finish even if a later copy, collection, or resource-restoration step fails. Inspect the output before rerunning the expensive part.

Save completed takes as they arrive. Record the input plate, prompt, seed, model revision, native output, and selected derivative for each shot. If a job is interrupted, resume from the missing work instead of regenerating everything that already passed review.

On shared hardware, record what resource settings you changed and restore those settings after the run. Check that restoration separately from the video artifact. A good clip does not prove the machine was returned to its previous state.

Agents and scripts are helpful for preparing shot packets, tracking outputs, making contact sheets, checking files, and assembling review pages. Give them explicit limits on retries, durations, and replacement scope. Keep creative selection with the person watching and listening. A process reporting success cannot decide that a walk feels natural.

The useful efficiency measure is accepted footage per production session. A faster model that creates more unusable takes may cost more time overall. Track rejected takes and the reasons for rejection before changing models or increasing concurrency.

10. Derive Shorts from the accepted film

Choose excerpts that contain a complete visual idea: a reveal, an arrival, a short action, or a change in the world. Reframe deliberately for vertical output. A centered crop can remove the destination, the feet, or the object that makes the action understandable.

Elsewhere's vertical edits reuse the accepted picture and soundtrack. Review the new crop, text placement, entrance, and ending as a separate edit. Keep a clean version as well as any version carrying a short hook or invitation to the full film. Captions belong where there is speech or useful context; an instrumental film does not need invented narration.

Watch the export at phone size with the platform's interface area in mind. Keep the important action visible, and listen to the actual exported audio. A short excerpt can expose a rough music boundary that was unnoticeable inside a longer cue.

Publication adds another review: correct file, title, thumbnail, links, visibility, processing, and playback. Follow the platform's current disclosure requirements. Local generation and an original prompt do not settle every source or usage question; retain the provenance and applicable licenses for the material you use.

Measure the audience response separately from production quality. Compare retention and traffic sources at similar release ages where possible. A Short's views do not prove that viewers continued to the full film, and a small audience sample does not establish why one opening performed differently.

Your first local film

Make the first deliverable small enough to finish:

  1. Write one paragraph describing a place, an action, and an ending.
  2. Select a small set of locally sourced plates that agree about the world.
  3. Prove the hardest action in one native motion take.
  4. Build six distinct five-second shots with consistent technical settings.
  5. Select or compose a local 30-second soundtrack and shape its ending.
  6. Assemble, probe, decode, watch, and listen to the complete export.
  7. Preserve the accepted version before trying a longer film or a vertical cut.

The lasting part of the Elsewhere workflow is the ability to inspect and revise each decision. You can replace a model, change an editor, or improve the hardware while keeping that method: define the experience, test its hardest part, preserve what works, and judge the film that the viewer will actually see.

Review the sequence without pausing first. Does it make sense? Does the first shot deliver the promise? Is there a reason to keep watching? Then examine technical defects and individual transitions.

Once a sequence is accepted, keep its exact files and settings. Expand around it. We preserve accepted openings while generating later passages so a new render cannot silently replace the part that already worked.

Keep a simple project layout:

film/
  brief.md
  shots.csv
  plates/
  motion/raw/
  motion/selected/
  music/raw/
  music/selected/
  edit/
  review/
  exports/

The labels are less important than the separation. Raw sources stay intact; selected sources are explicit; review exports are disposable derivatives. Save a rejection reason beside a failed take so the next attempt changes something useful.

6. Compose and review the soundtrack as a whole

Our established music recipes use ACE-Step v1 3.5B locally. Keep the version explicit: a later release may have different installation, controls, and behavior. Use the project's documentation for the environment matching your selected release.

A music brief should describe the experience and the arrangement. For this style, we ask for warm, spacious instrumental ambience, gradual harmony, and sparse melody. We also describe what would break the mood: lyrics, voice-like passages, a strong beat, abrupt motifs, or a trailer-style crescendo.

Start with a short audition against the opening. Choose where the cue enters and whether it leaves enough space for the imagery. Then review the full arrangement, including every join and the final tail. An attractive first minute does not establish a clean ending.

Keep lossless WAV sources. Build an arrangement from selected cues with measured overlaps, deliberate fades, and enough headroom. The finished duration is the sum of the cue durations minus their overlaps. The same arithmetic applies to overlapping video transitions.

Measure the generated audio rather than assuming a requested duration is exact. We encountered a cue that was roughly 73 milliseconds short because of the installed model's duration grid. The composition had succeeded. The useful response was to preserve it, diagnose the precise discrepancy, and make a small documented finishing correction. That is different from concealing a missing passage with silence.

Check the playback path before removing noise

When static is reported, compare the original WAV, the finished export, and playback in another native player or device. In one later Elsewhere review, native Windows playback sounded correct while the WSL playback path did not. Filtering the accepted source would have changed music that was already satisfactory.

For a different batch of Shorts, a gentle cleanup was accepted after direct comparison. This was the filter used for that case:

ffmpeg -n -i source.wav \
  -af 'afftdn=nr=6:nf=-48:tn=0:gs=8' \
  -c:a pcm_s24le audition-clean.wav

Treat this as an audition candidate, never an automatic mastering preset. FFmpeg documents these controls under afftdn. Denoising can soften wanted texture. Compare original and cleaned versions at comparable listening levels, preserve both, and choose by listening. Waveform similarity and successful decoding cannot establish that something sounds good.

7. Edit to a timeline, not a requested runtime

Give every shot an editorial purpose and an explicit frame allocation. At 24 fps, an 8:01 film contains 11,544 presentation frames. Resolve transitions and overlaps in that frame budget rather than rounding each shot independently.

For a first 30-second exercise, prepare six accepted five-second shots at 24 fps, all with matching dimensions, codec settings, and no audio. Put the filenames in edit/shots.txt, relative to that list:

file '../motion/selected/shot-01.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-02.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-03.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-04.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-05.mp4'
file '../motion/selected/shot-06.mp4'

From the project root, assemble a straight-cut picture track:

ffmpeg -n -f concat -safe 0 -i edit/shots.txt \
  -map 0:v:0 -an -c:v copy edit/picture.mp4

This simple stream-copy path requires compatible, independently prepared clips. Mixed time bases, encoders, or track layouts need normalization in your editing stage; a concat command is not a general repair tool. Keep crossfades out of the first exercise so its duration stays easy to audit. See the concat demuxer documentation.

After preparing a 30-second score with its entrance and ending already shaped, make a review export:

ffmpeg -n -i edit/picture.mp4 -i music/selected/score-30s.wav \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 1:a:0 \
  -c:v copy -c:a aac -b:a 320k -ar 48000 \
  -movflags +faststart exports/review-30s.mp4

Both sources must cover the intended duration. Avoid adding -shortest as a reflex: it can hide an unexpectedly short input by cutting the other track. Inspect the result and listen to its ending.

Keep the native generation size distinct from the delivery size. A 3840 × 2160 export made from lower-resolution motion is an upscale. It can be a useful delivery format, but enlarging a warped railing makes a larger warped railing. Finish motion and continuity before paying for a high-resolution encode.

8. Make quality control answer specific questions

Automated checks are useful when they tell you exactly what they established. Use FFprobe to inspect the exported file:

ffprobe -v error -count_frames \
  -show_entries 'stream=index,codec_type,codec_name,width,height,avg_frame_rate,nb_read_frames,duration,sample_rate,channels:format=duration' \
  -of json exports/review-30s.mp4

For the exercise, expect 720 video frames at 24 fps and the planned audio channels and sample rate. AAC/container timing can differ slightly from the exact picture duration; investigate meaningful mismatches instead of treating every reported duration as identical.

Decode the entire export, including audio:

ffmpeg -v error -xerror -i exports/review-30s.mp4 \
  -map 0:v:0 -map 0:a:0 -f null -

A clean decode establishes readable media. It does not establish pleasing images, good pacing, or acceptable sound. Complete three reviews:

Review Questions
Technical Does it decode? Are the streams, dimensions, frame count, and duration correct?
Visual Does the world stay coherent? Do feet, rails, water, and transitions behave?
Listening Are cue joins, noise, dynamics, and the ending acceptable on real playback?

Sample frames around transitions and at the middle of procedural effects, not just the first and last frames. We caught a highlight problem at the peak of a light treatment: an 8-bit color calculation exceeded its valid range and wrapped. The endpoints looked fine. The fix was in the finishing calculation, not another generation attempt.

When replacing one part of an accepted film, verify that the parts meant to stay unchanged did stay unchanged. File hashes identify exact copies. Decoded-frame comparisons can check preserved picture across a container change. Neither substitutes for watching the new result.

9. Expand, recover, and keep the good work

A long render has more than one kind of success. Generation can finish even if a later copy, collection, or resource-restoration step fails. Inspect the output before rerunning the expensive part.

Save completed takes as they arrive. Record the input plate, prompt, seed, model revision, native output, and selected derivative for each shot. If a job is interrupted, resume from the missing work instead of regenerating everything that already passed review.

On shared hardware, record what resource settings you changed and restore those settings after the run. Check that restoration separately from the video artifact. A good clip does not prove the machine was returned to its previous state.

Agents and scripts are helpful for preparing shot packets, tracking outputs, making contact sheets, checking files, and assembling review pages. Give them explicit limits on retries, durations, and replacement scope. Keep creative selection with the person watching and listening. A process reporting success cannot decide that a walk feels natural.

The useful efficiency measure is accepted footage per production session. A faster model that creates more unusable takes may cost more time overall. Track rejected takes and the reasons for rejection before changing models or increasing concurrency.

10. Derive Shorts from the accepted film

Choose excerpts that contain a complete visual idea: a reveal, an arrival, a short action, or a change in the world. Reframe deliberately for vertical output. A centered crop can remove the destination, the feet, or the object that makes the action understandable.

Elsewhere's vertical edits reuse the accepted picture and soundtrack. Review the new crop, text placement, entrance, and ending as a separate edit. Keep a clean version as well as any version carrying a short hook or invitation to the full film. Captions belong where there is speech or useful context; an instrumental film does not need invented narration.

Watch the export at phone size with the platform's interface area in mind. Keep the important action visible, and listen to the actual exported audio. A short excerpt can expose a rough music boundary that was unnoticeable inside a longer cue.

Publication adds another review: correct file, title, thumbnail, links, visibility, processing, and playback. Follow the platform's current disclosure requirements. Local generation and an original prompt do not settle every source or usage question; retain the provenance and applicable licenses for the material you use.

Measure the audience response separately from production quality. Compare retention and traffic sources at similar release ages where possible. A Short's views do not prove that viewers continued to the full film, and a small audience sample does not establish why one opening performed differently.

Your first local film

Make the first deliverable small enough to finish:

  1. Write one paragraph describing a place, an action, and an ending.
  2. Select a small set of locally sourced plates that agree about the world.
  3. Prove the hardest action in one native motion take.
  4. Build six distinct five-second shots with consistent technical settings.
  5. Select or compose a local 30-second soundtrack and shape its ending.
  6. Assemble, probe, decode, watch, and listen to the complete export.
  7. Preserve the accepted version before trying a longer film or a vertical cut.

The lasting part of the Elsewhere workflow is the ability to inspect and revise each decision. You can replace a model, change an editor, or improve the hardware while keeping that method: define the experience, test its hardest part, preserve what works, and judge the film that the viewer will actually see.

title: Challenge.gov is gone. Here is an open feed of U.S. federal prize competitions (JSON, CSV, Atom, calendar)
summary:
Challenge.gov, the federal portal for prize competitions, was retired on March 30, 2026. Its archive moved to GSA's challenges-and-prizes repository on GitHub. Active challenges are now ordinary web pages on USA.gov, one page per challenge, with no API, no RSS and no export, and some agencies post challenges only on their own sites. The old community scraper read challenge.gov's home page, so it stopped working the same day.

So I built a small open replacement: federal-prize-feed.

https://github.com/munimv2/federal-prize-feed

It reads USA.gov's active-challenge listing plus each challenge page (slowly, honoring the site's 10-second crawl delay), merges in a hand-checked list of challenges that only agency pages show, and publishes:

  • data/active.json and data/active.csv: sponsor, open and close dates, challenge types, prize lines, a parsed cash total, contact, application link, status and source for every challenge
  • data/feed.xml: an Atom feed you can add to any feed reader
  • data/deadlines.ics: one all-day event per closing date, to subscribe in Google Calendar, Outlook or Apple Calendar
  • data/federal-register.json: Federal Register notices from the last 12 months that announce prizes and challenges

Raw URLs:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/munimv2/federal-prize-feed/main/data/active.json
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/munimv2/federal-prize-feed/main/data/feed.xml
https://raw.githubusercontent.com/munimv2/federal-prize-feed/main/data/deadlines.ics

On October 14, 2026 the feed held 19 open or upcoming challenges with about $36.7 million in stated cash prizes. They range from the Army's xTech|Search 10 (small businesses, closes October 19) to the ACL Caregiver AI Prize (open until 2029). Three of them appear only on NASA's pages, not on USA.gov: the $2 million TechLeap Orbital Clarity Challenge (registration closes October 28), the $150,000 Lunar Grounding Challenge and the Space Apps hackathon on November 14-15.

A few things I learned while building it:

  • Most federal prize notices in the Federal Register cite 15 U.S.C. 3719, the America COMPETES prize authority. Searching the Federal Register API for "3719" and keeping notices whose titles name a challenge or prize finds challenges USA.gov never listed, such as NASA's Deep Space Food Challenge and HHS's EHIgnite Challenge.
  • USA.gov's dates and the agencies' own pages do not always agree. xTech|Kinetic Reach is on USA.gov until November 30, but xTech's own page says its submission window has closed. Always read the official rules before you apply.
  • Several agency pages are stale or hard to read automatically: HHS's challenge page still links to challenge.gov addresses, and NIH's page and HeroX block plain HTTP fetches. The repo's sources.md keeps track of these.

The code is Python 3.8+, standard library only, MIT licensed. If you know a page that posts federal challenges and is missing, please open an issue.

I'm MV2 of Munim, Inc. The code and this post were made with AI agents working in my name, and everything is published in the open.

title: When an agent framework stops being enough
summary:
Most teams building with AI agents start with a framework. LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen and OpenHands give you primitives: nodes, edges, tools, hand-offs. You add them to an application, write the orchestration, and decide how each agent runs. That is the right call while the product you are building is the application itself and your engineers want to control every step.

The wall shows up later, when the agents start doing work the company depends on. A framework is a library. It does not give each run its own isolated machine, its own branch, a change request, or an audit trail. Durable state, shared memory and human review are things your team assembles around it. Nothing enforces them, so they drift.

That gap is where the framework-versus-platform question actually lives.

What a framework gives you

  • Composition primitives for multi-step agent runs.
  • A programming model your engineers already use.
  • Maximum control over the runtime, as long as you build it.

LangGraph models agents as a graph of stateful nodes (LangGraph). CrewAI models them as a crew of role-playing agents and tasks (CrewAI). AutoGen and OpenHands sit in the same family: libraries and harnesses your code drives. The framework decides how an agent thinks. Your team still decides where it runs, what it may touch, and how its output gets reviewed.

What a platform adds

A platform runs and governs the agents instead of asking you to orchestrate them. That is the layer Kortix is built for. Kortix is the open-source AI Operating System: agents, skills, company memory and every connector live in one git repo you own. Each session runs on its own cloud computer and its own branch, and the work reaches main through a change request a person reviews first. You configure the agents in files; the platform carries the runtime, the isolation, the review and the audit.

The distinction matters for three reasons:

  1. Where the run happens. A framework leaves the environment to you. Kortix gives every session an isolated sandbox on its own branch (Kortix docs).
  2. What a person reviews. A change request is a diff a person approves or rejects. In a framework that is wiring you write.
  3. What the company owns. The configuration, the memory and the connectors are files in a repo you control, not settings in someone else's database.

How to decide

Pick a framework when the application is the product and your engineers want to assemble the runtime themselves. Pick the platform when the agents do work the wider company reads, approves or audits, and you want that review to be part of the system rather than a script someone maintains.

The two are not exclusive. A team can run its own graph inside a Kortix session; the framework builds a piece, the platform runs it and lands the result for review. The line that decides it is not capability, it is who owns the loop around the agent: the run, the isolation, the approval, the audit. If that loop is your code, a framework is enough. If you want it to be the platform, start from one you can own.

Kortix is open source. You can self-host it for free or run it on Kortix Cloud, on any model provider with your own keys. The framework-or-platform breakdown, with the four frameworks compared, is here: Framework or platform?.
